sectionTitle: Hazards and uses of radioactive emissions and of background radiation (physics only)

specStatements.text: Background radiation is around us all of the time. It comes from:
• natural sources such as rocks and cosmic rays from space
• man-made sources such as the fallout from nuclear weapons testing and nuclear accidents.
The level of background radiation and radiation dose may be affected by occupation and/or location.
Radiation dose is measured in sieverts (Sv)
Students will not need to recall the unit of radiation dose.
Radioactive isotopes have a very wide range of half-life values.
Students should be able to explain why the hazards associated with radioactive material differ according to the half-life involved.
Nuclear radiations are used in medicine for the:
• control or destruction of unwanted tissue.
• describe and evaluate the uses of nuclear radiations for exploration of internal organs, and for control or destruction of unwanted tissue
• evaluate the perceived risks of using nuclear radiations in relation to given data and consequences.

scopeNotes.statement: Students will not need to recall the unit of radiation dose.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: No item asks students to name or select the unit of radiation dose from memory. Wherever dose appears — in the concepts, in q07, q08, q09 and q17 — the unit is supplied in the wording ("a dose of 4.5 mSv", "1000 millisieverts (mSv) = 1 sievert (Sv)"), and the student is asked instead to interpret what a dose value means, to convert between millisieverts and sieverts, or to compare two given doses. The sievert is defined in c08 and c09 as supporting information so that given data can be read with understanding, not as something to be recalled in an examination.

concepts.definition: The low-level ionising radiation that is around us all of the time. It comes from natural sources such as rocks and cosmic rays from space, and from man-made sources such as the fallout from nuclear weapons testing and nuclear accidents.

Sources that are not produced by human activity, such as rocks and cosmic rays from space. Rocks in the ground and in building materials contain radioactive isotopes, so a low level of radiation is always present.

Ionising radiation that reaches the Earth from space. The atmosphere absorbs a large part of it, so the dose received from cosmic rays is greater at high altitude, where there is less atmosphere above you.
Sources that exist because of human activity. The specification gives the fallout from nuclear weapons testing and from nuclear accidents as the examples.
Radioactive material thrown into the atmosphere by a nuclear weapons test or a nuclear accident, which then spreads and settles onto land and water, adding to the background radiation there.

concepts.term: Effect of occupation on radiation dose
concepts.definition: The radiation dose a person receives may be affected by the job they do. People who work with radioactive sources or with radiation-producing equipment, such as radiographers and workers in the nuclear industry, may receive a higher dose than the rest of the population, so their dose is monitored.

concepts.term: Effect of location on radiation dose
concepts.definition: The level of background radiation may be affected by where a person is. Places built on rock types that contain more radioactive isotopes have a higher background level, and places at high altitude receive a larger dose from cosmic rays.

A measure of the risk of harm to the body resulting from exposure to ionising radiation. Radiation dose is measured in sieverts (Sv). It is not the same as activity, which counts the decays per second in a source.

The sievert (Sv) is the unit of radiation dose. Everyday doses are small, so they are usually quoted in millisieverts: 1000 millisieverts (mSv) = 1 sievert (Sv). To convert a dose in mSv to Sv, divide by 1000.
Radioactive isotopes have a very wide range of half-life values, from small fractions of a second for some isotopes to thousands of millions of years for others.

For a given number of undecayed nuclei, a short half-life means many decays happen each second, so the activity is high and the radiation emitted is intense. The hazard is severe but short-lived, because the activity falls away quickly.

For a given number of undecayed nuclei, a long half-life means fewer decays each second, so the activity is lower. The hazard is less intense but lasts far longer, because the material stays radioactive for many years, so contamination of land, water or a workplace remains a problem for a very long time.

A use of nuclear radiation in medicine in which a small amount of a radioactive isotope is swallowed, injected or inhaled. The radiation it emits passes out of the body and is detected outside, so doctors can follow where the substance goes and see how an organ is working, without surgery.

concepts.term: Control or destruction of unwanted tissue (radiotherapy)
concepts.definition: A use of nuclear radiation in medicine in which radiation is directed at unwanted tissue, such as a tumour, to control its growth or destroy it. The dose is concentrated on the tumour, but healthy tissue nearby still receives some radiation.

concepts.term: Evaluating a use of nuclear radiation
concepts.definition: Judging a use by setting its benefits against its drawbacks: the information a scan gives or the tissue a treatment destroys, weighed against the dose received, the possible damage to healthy cells and the alternatives available.

The risk people believe a use of nuclear radiation carries is often different from the risk shown by data on doses and consequences. An evaluation must use the data given — for example comparing a dose with the background dose received anyway — rather than the strength of feeling about radiation.

concepts.term: Choosing an isotope for a medical use
concepts.definition: The half-life and the type of radiation determine how hazardous an isotope is and what it can be used for. A tracer needs a half-life long enough for the scan but short enough that the activity falls quickly afterwards, and radiation penetrating enough to leave the body and reach a detector.

misconceptions.question: Is there any radiation around you right now if there has been no nuclear accident nearby?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. Background radiation is around us all of the time.
misconceptions.misconception: There is no radiation around normally — it only appears somewhere after a nuclear accident or a leak.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Radiation is almost only mentioned in the news in connection with accidents and weapons, so students associate its presence with disaster rather than with everyday life.
misconceptions.correction: Background radiation is present continuously and everywhere. It comes from natural sources such as rocks and cosmic rays from space, as well as from man-made sources. An accident can raise the level in a place, but it does not create radiation where there was none before.

misconceptions.question: Fallout contains atoms of elements found in nature. Does that make it a natural source of background radiation?
misconceptions.correct: No. Fallout from nuclear weapons testing and from nuclear accidents is a man-made source.
misconceptions.misconception: Fallout is a natural source, because the radioactive atoms in it are just elements that occur naturally anyway.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students classify by what a substance is made of rather than by how it came to be there, and they know uranium is a naturally occurring element.
misconceptions.correction: The classification is by origin. Rocks and cosmic rays from space were there without human action, so they are natural. Fallout is spread across the Earth because people tested weapons or because a reactor failed, so it is man-made.

misconceptions.question: Are the ordinary rocks under a house a source of background radiation?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. Rocks are given by the specification as an example of a natural source.
misconceptions.misconception: Ordinary rocks are not radioactive — only uranium ore in a mine is.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students meet radioactivity as something special and rare, kept in a lead box in a laboratory, so they do not expect the ground itself to be a source.
misconceptions.correction: Rocks contain small amounts of radioactive isotopes, so they emit radiation continuously. How much depends on the rock type, which is one reason the background level varies from place to place.

misconceptions.question: Would there still be background radiation if no one had ever built a reactor or tested a weapon?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. Natural sources such as rocks and cosmic rays from space would still be there.
misconceptions.misconception: Background radiation exists because of nuclear technology — it is all left over from power stations and bombs.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The man-made sources are the ones students hear about, so they assume those sources account for the whole of the background.
misconceptions.correction: Background radiation has two kinds of source. The natural ones — rocks and cosmic rays from space — have always been present. Man-made sources such as the fallout from weapons testing and nuclear accidents add to that background; they are not the whole of it.

misconceptions.question: Is the background radiation level the same wherever you live and whatever job you do?
misconceptions.correct: No. The level of background radiation and radiation dose may be affected by occupation and/or location.
misconceptions.misconception: Background radiation is a fixed amount that is the same for everybody, everywhere.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word 'background' suggests a constant baseline, and textbook questions often quote a single average value for a country as if it applied to every person in it.
misconceptions.correction: A quoted background figure is an average. A person living where the rock contains more radioactive isotopes, or at high altitude, or working with radioactive sources, receives a different dose from the average.

misconceptions.question: Does living high up a mountain reduce the radiation dose you receive from background radiation?
misconceptions.correct: No. The dose from cosmic rays is greater at high altitude.
misconceptions.misconception: Higher up you are further from the radioactive rocks in the ground, so you must get less radiation.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students correctly learn that radiation gets weaker with distance from a source, then apply that idea to the ground while forgetting the second natural source named in the specification.
misconceptions.correction: There is a source above as well as below. Cosmic rays come from space and are absorbed by the atmosphere, so at high altitude, with less atmosphere overhead, more of them reach you and the dose from them is higher.

misconceptions.question: A dose is given as 2 mSv. Does that tell you how many nuclei are decaying each second?
misconceptions.correct: No. That is activity, measured in becquerels. Radiation dose, measured in sieverts, is a measure of the risk of harm from the radiation received.
misconceptions.misconception: Sieverts and becquerels both measure how radioactive something is, so a dose in sieverts tells you the decays per second.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both quantities are met in the same topic and both get bigger when there is 'more radiation', so students merge them into a single idea of strength.
misconceptions.correction: Activity is a property of the source: decays per second, in becquerels. Dose is a property of the person exposed: the risk of harm from the radiation their body received, in sieverts. The same source gives different doses to people standing at different distances.

misconceptions.question: A dose is 250 mSv. Is that 2.5 Sv?
misconceptions.correct: No. 1000 millisieverts (mSv) = 1 sievert (Sv), so 250 mSv = 0.25 Sv.
misconceptions.misconception: 'Milli' means a hundredth, so you divide by 100 — or a tenth, so you divide by 10.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students recall that centimetres and metres differ by 100 and transfer that factor to any prefix conversion instead of using the relationship given.
misconceptions.correction: Use the relationship as it is stated: 1000 mSv = 1 sievert. So a dose in mSv is divided by 1000 to give sieverts, and a dose in Sv is multiplied by 1000 to give millisieverts.

misconceptions.question: Two sources hold the same number of undecayed nuclei. Is the one with the longer half-life giving out more radiation each second?
misconceptions.correct: No. A longer half-life means fewer decays each second, so a lower activity now.
misconceptions.misconception: A long half-life means the material is more radioactive, so it must be the more dangerous of the two.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Long' is read as 'more', and students know a long-lived waste isotope is described as dangerous, so they conclude that long half-life equals high activity.
misconceptions.correction: Half-life is the time for the activity, or the number of undecayed nuclei, to halve. A long half-life means the nuclei decay slowly, so the activity is lower now — but the material stays radioactive for a very long time, which is a different kind of hazard.

misconceptions.question: An isotope has a half-life of a few minutes. Does that mean it is harmless?
misconceptions.correct: No. A very short half-life means a very high activity while it lasts.
misconceptions.misconception: Something with a short half-life decays away almost at once, so it cannot do any harm.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students focus on how long the hazard lasts and ignore how intense it is, because half-life is taught as a time rather than as a rate of decay.
misconceptions.correction: A short half-life means a large number of decays each second, so the radiation emitted is intense and the hazard while it lasts is severe. What is true is that the hazard does not persist: the activity falls quickly, which is why short half-life isotopes are chosen for use inside the body.

misconceptions.question: Are the half-lives of different radioactive isotopes all roughly similar?
misconceptions.correct: No. Radioactive isotopes have a very wide range of half-life values.
misconceptions.misconception: Half-lives are all about the same order of size — a few years, or at most a few hundred years.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Practice questions use convenient values such as 2 days or 5 years, so students never meet the extremes and assume the range is narrow.
misconceptions.correction: Half-lives range from tiny fractions of a second to thousands of millions of years. That range is exactly why the hazard from different radioactive materials differs so much.

misconceptions.question: Alpha radiation is the most strongly ionising. Does that make an alpha emitter the best choice for a medical tracer?
misconceptions.correct: No. Alpha radiation would be absorbed inside the body and would never reach the detector.
misconceptions.misconception: The most ionising radiation must give the clearest picture, so use an alpha emitter for a tracer.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students carry over 'strongly ionising means a strong effect' from the hazard topic without asking what has to happen for a tracer to work at all.
misconceptions.correction: A tracer has to be detected outside the body, so its radiation must be penetrating enough to get out — gamma radiation. Being strongly ionising is a drawback here, not an advantage: alpha radiation absorbed by the patient's tissue delivers dose without producing any image.

misconceptions.question: In radiotherapy, is only the tumour affected by the radiation?
misconceptions.correct: No. Healthy tissue in the path of the radiation also receives a dose.
misconceptions.misconception: The beam is aimed at the tumour, so healthy cells are untouched and the treatment carries no risk.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Diagrams show a single arrow ending at the tumour, which suggests the radiation stops there rather than passing through tissue on the way in and out.
misconceptions.correction: Radiation reaching the tumour has to pass through healthy tissue, and some of that tissue is damaged. Treatment is planned to keep this as small as possible — for example by directing beams at the tumour from several different directions so the tumour receives a high dose while each path through healthy tissue receives much less — but the risk is reduced, not removed.

misconceptions.question: Radiation can damage cells and cause cancer. Does that mean medical uses of nuclear radiation should always be refused?
misconceptions.correct: No. The risk has to be evaluated against the data given and the consequences of not treating.
misconceptions.misconception: Any exposure to nuclear radiation is unacceptable, so no dose is ever worth taking.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The hazards of radiation are taught vividly and separately from the benefits, and public feeling about radiation is stronger than about most other medical risks.
misconceptions.correction: An evaluation compares both sides using the figures given. A scan dose that is a fraction of the dose received from background radiation in a year may allow a disease to be found and treated, and an untreated tumour may be far more likely to kill the patient than the treatment is to harm them.

misconceptions.question: After a tracer scan, is the patient radioactive for the rest of their life?
misconceptions.correct: No. A tracer isotope is chosen so that its activity falls quickly after the scan.
misconceptions.misconception: Once you have been given a radioactive substance you stay radioactive permanently.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students think of contamination as something that soaks in and stays, and they do not connect the choice of isotope with how long the activity lasts.
misconceptions.correction: The isotope used has a half-life long enough for the scan to be completed but short enough that the activity falls away rapidly afterwards, so the dose the patient receives is limited.

misconceptions.question: Do cosmic rays only reach us from the Sun, so that there are none at night?
misconceptions.correct: No. Cosmic rays reach the Earth from space, and background radiation is around us all of the time.
misconceptions.misconception: Cosmic rays are just part of sunlight, so you only receive them when the Sun is shining on you.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The Sun is the only object in space students routinely link with radiation reaching the Earth, so 'from space' is read as 'from the Sun'.
misconceptions.correction: Cosmic rays arrive from space in general, not only from the Sun, and background radiation is present continuously. Their contribution to dose depends on where you are — for example it is greater at high altitude — not on the time of day.

misconceptions.question: A patient's dose is given as 0.5 mSv. Is that the mass of radioactive material they took in?
misconceptions.correct: No. Radiation dose measures the risk of harm from the radiation the body received.
misconceptions.misconception: Dose is like a dose of medicine — it is the amount of radioactive substance given to the person.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The everyday meaning of 'dose' is a quantity of a substance, so students read the word as an amount of material rather than as an effect on the body.
misconceptions.correction: Radiation dose is not an amount of substance. It is a measure of the risk of harm resulting from the body being exposed to ionising radiation, and it is measured in sieverts. A person standing near a source receives a dose without any material entering them at all.

misconceptions.question: To change a dose of 3 mSv into sieverts, do you multiply by 1000?
misconceptions.correct: No. You divide by 1000, giving 0.003 Sv.
misconceptions.misconception: Converting units always means multiplying by the number in the relationship.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students see '1000' in the relationship and reach for multiplication without checking whether the answer should come out larger or smaller.
misconceptions.correction: 1000 mSv = 1 Sv, so a millisievert is the smaller unit. A dose expressed in the smaller unit gives a smaller number in sieverts, so divide by 1000. Check the answer is smaller than the number you started with.

misconceptions.question: Does the half-life of a spilled radioactive material affect how long the area stays a hazard?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. The longer the half-life, the longer the material stays significantly radioactive.
misconceptions.misconception: Half-life is just a number used in decay calculations; how dangerous a spill is depends only on how much was spilled.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Half-life is usually met in graph and calculation questions, so students treat it as a piece of arithmetic rather than as the thing that decides how long a hazard lasts.
misconceptions.correction: Half-life sets both how intense the emission is now and how long the material remains a problem. A spill with a half-life of hours becomes safe within days; one with a half-life of tens of years contaminates the area for a human lifetime.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about background radiation is correct?

options.text: It is around us all of the time, from natural and man-made sources.
options.rationale: Background radiation is continuously present and has both natural sources, such as rocks and cosmic rays from space, and man-made sources, such as fallout.

options.text: It is only present in places affected by a nuclear accident.
options.rationale: Students link radiation with disaster because that is when it is reported, so they think it appears only where something has gone wrong.

options.text: It exists only because humans have used nuclear technology.
options.rationale: The man-made sources are the memorable ones, so students assume the whole background is left over from reactors and weapons.

options.text: It is only found in places where uranium-bearing rocks occur.
options.rationale: Students who know rocks are a source over-restrict it to ore-bearing ground and forget cosmic rays and man-made sources entirely.

mcqs.stem: Which of these sources of background radiation is a natural source?

options.text: Fallout left by nuclear weapons testing
options.rationale: Students classify by what the material is rather than how it got there, and the isotopes in fallout are elements found in nature.

options.text: Cosmic rays arriving from outer space
options.rationale: The specification names cosmic rays from space, alongside rocks, as an example of a natural source of background radiation.

options.text: Emissions released in a nuclear accident
options.rationale: An accident is not planned, so students read it as something that 'just happened' and count it as natural.

options.text: Fuel rods used in a nuclear reactor core
options.rationale: Uranium is a naturally occurring element, so students treat processed reactor fuel as a natural source of background radiation.

mcqs.stem: People who live high up a mountain receive a larger radiation dose from cosmic rays than people at sea level. Why?

options.text: They are further from the radioactive rocks in the ground.
options.rationale: Students apply 'further from the source means less radiation' to the ground and forget that this question is about the source above them.

options.text: Cosmic rays are produced by the thinner air found high up.
options.rationale: Students who know the effect depends on altitude invent a mechanism in which the atmosphere makes the radiation rather than absorbs it.

options.text: There is less atmosphere above them to absorb the cosmic rays.
options.rationale: Cosmic rays come from space and are absorbed as they pass through the atmosphere, so less overhead atmosphere means a greater dose.

options.text: They are closer to the Sun, the only source of cosmic rays.
options.rationale: Students equate 'from space' with 'from the Sun', and a few kilometres of altitude feels like getting closer to it.

mcqs.stem: Which pair are both man-made sources of background radiation?

options.text: Fallout from weapons testing and cosmic rays
options.rationale: Students who think cosmic rays are connected with human activity in space, or simply cannot place them, pair them with a man-made source.

options.text: Rocks in the ground and fallout from nuclear accidents
options.rationale: Students who believe only mined or processed material is radioactive treat rocks as something people have made hazardous.

options.text: Cosmic rays from space and rocks in the ground
options.rationale: This is the natural pair; students who read the question as 'which pair belong together' rather than 'which are man-made' choose it.

options.text: Fallout from weapons testing and nuclear accidents
options.rationale: These are exactly the two examples of man-made sources given by the specification.

mcqs.stem: A radiographer wears a badge at work that records the radiation dose she receives, and her total dose each year is checked. Which statement best explains why this is done?

options.text: Her occupation can raise the radiation dose she receives.
options.rationale: The specification states that radiation dose may be affected by occupation; working with radiation-producing equipment can raise her dose above that of the general population.

options.text: Everyone receives the same dose, so all workers are checked.
options.rationale: Students who think the background level is a fixed amount for everybody cannot see why one job would be singled out.

options.text: The badge lowers the dose the radiographer receives at work.
options.rationale: Students confuse a monitoring device with a shield, assuming that anything worn for radiation safety must block radiation.

options.text: The badge measures the activity of the sources in becquerels.
options.rationale: Students merge dose and activity into one idea of 'how much radiation', so they expect the badge to read the source's activity.

mcqs.stem: Two identical houses are built in different parts of the country, one on granite and one on clay. Which statement about the background radiation in the two houses is correct?

options.text: Both houses have exactly the same background level.
options.rationale: Students treat 'background' as a single fixed national value that cannot depend on where a house happens to stand.

options.text: Background level can differ because the rocks differ.
options.rationale: Rocks are a natural source of background radiation and different rock types contain different amounts of radioactive isotopes, so location affects the level.

options.text: The clay house has more because clay is denser rock.
options.rationale: Students reach for a physical property they can name and assume more tightly packed material must give out more radiation.

options.text: Neither house has any, since rocks are not radioactive.
options.rationale: Students who think radioactivity only belongs to laboratory sources deny that ordinary ground emits anything at all.

mcqs.stem: A worker's radiation dose for one year is recorded as 3.6 millisieverts (mSv). What does this dose tell you?

options.text: The number of decays each second in the source.
options.rationale: Dose and activity are met together, so students read any radiation measurement as a count of decays per second.

options.text: The energy stored in the radioactive source used.
options.rationale: Students reach for energy because it is the quantity they most often attach to a number in physics, and radiation is described as carrying energy.

options.text: The risk of harm from the radiation received.
options.rationale: Radiation dose, measured in sieverts, is a measure of the risk of harm resulting from the body being exposed to ionising radiation.

options.text: The mass of radioactive material absorbed.
options.rationale: The everyday meaning of 'dose' is an amount of a substance, so students read it as material taken into the body.

mcqs.stem: A patient receives a radiation dose of 4.5 mSv. Given that 1000 millisieverts (mSv) = 1 sievert (Sv), what is this dose in sieverts?

options.rationale: The student divides by 10, treating 'milli' as though it meant a tenth.

options.text: 45 Sv
options.rationale: The student moves the decimal point one place the wrong way, producing an answer larger than the value in the smaller unit.
The student multiplies by 1000 instead of dividing, using the number in the relationship without checking the direction.

mcqs.stem: In one year worker P receives a dose of 0.8 mSv and worker Q receives a dose of 0.0015 Sv. Use 1000 millisieverts (mSv) = 1 sievert (Sv). Which comparison is correct?

options.text: Q receives the higher dose, about twice that of P.
options.rationale: 0.0015 Sv = 1.5 mSv, and 1.5 mSv is a little under twice 0.8 mSv, so Q receives roughly double P's dose.

options.text: P receives the higher dose, as 0.8 is the larger number.
options.rationale: The student compares the figures without converting, so the mixed units are never made the same.

options.text: The two doses are equal once the units are converted.
options.rationale: The student converts one value but rounds 1.5 mSv down to 'about 1', then judges the two to be close enough to call equal.

options.text: Q receives the higher dose, about 1000 times that of P.
options.rationale: The student converts Q's dose by multiplying by 1000 a second time, arriving at a figure a thousand times too large.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about the half-lives of radioactive isotopes is correct?

options.text: They are all of a similar length, around a few years.
options.rationale: Practice questions use convenient values of a few days or years, so students assume that is the whole range.

options.text: They range from fractions of a second to billions of years.
options.rationale: Radioactive isotopes have a very wide range of half-life values, which is why the hazards they present differ so greatly.

options.text: The most hazardous isotopes always have the longest ones.
options.rationale: Students associate 'long-lived nuclear waste' with danger and conclude that a long half-life always means greater hazard.

options.text: Every isotope of a given element has the same half-life.
options.rationale: Students expect a property to belong to the element rather than to the particular isotope, as chemical properties do.

mcqs.stem: Two sealed sources contain the same number of undecayed nuclei. Source X has a half-life of 8 days and source Y has a half-life of 1600 years. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Y is more hazardous now because its half-life is longer.
options.rationale: 'Long' is read as 'more radioactive', so students expect the long-lived source to emit more radiation now.

options.text: X is completely harmless because it decays away fast.
options.rationale: Students judge the hazard only by how long it lasts and overlook how intense the emission is while it lasts.

options.text: X gives the higher activity now, but for a shorter time.
options.rationale: With equal numbers of nuclei, the shorter half-life means more decays each second now, so X is more intense but its activity falls away quickly.

options.text: Y decays faster now, so it releases more radiation today.
options.rationale: Students who read half-life as a measure of speed rather than of time invert the relationship and call the long half-life 'faster'.

mcqs.stem: Radioactive material is spilled on a laboratory floor. Why is a spill of an isotope with a half-life of 30 years a longer-term problem than a spill of one with a half-life of 6 hours?

options.text: The 30-year isotope emits far more radiation each second.
options.rationale: Students who think a long half-life means more radioactive explain the persistent hazard by a higher activity instead.

options.text: The 6-hour isotope cannot emit any radiation at all.
options.rationale: Students who treat a short half-life as meaning 'gone immediately' conclude that such a source is never a hazard.

options.text: Half-life does not affect how long contamination lasts.
options.rationale: Students who only meet half-life in calculations treat it as arithmetic rather than as what sets the lifetime of a hazard.

options.text: It stays significantly radioactive for many decades.
options.rationale: A 30-year half-life means the activity halves only once in 30 years, so the contaminated area remains hazardous for a human lifetime, while the 6-hour isotope decays to a low activity within days.

mcqs.stem: A patient is given a small amount of a radioactive substance so that doctors can follow where it goes inside the body. This is an example of:

options.text: exploring internal organs with nuclear radiation
options.rationale: This is the use the specification calls the exploration of internal organs: a tracer whose radiation escapes the body and is detected outside.

options.text: destroying unwanted tissue with nuclear radiation
options.rationale: Students know only one medical use in detail and assume any radiation given to a patient is there to kill tissue.

options.text: reducing the patient's background radiation dose
options.rationale: Students who have just met dose treat any medical procedure involving radiation as something done to manage the patient's dose.

options.text: making the patient permanently radioactive
options.rationale: Students think a substance taken into the body stays and keeps emitting, so they read the procedure as making the person radioactive for good.

mcqs.stem: Which combination of properties makes an isotope suitable for use as a medical tracer?

options.text: It emits alpha radiation, which is strongly ionising.
options.rationale: Students carry 'most ionising means strongest effect' across from the hazards topic without asking whether the radiation can leave the body.

options.text: It emits gamma radiation and has a short half-life.
options.rationale: Gamma radiation is penetrating enough to escape the body and reach a detector, and a short half-life means the activity falls quickly once the scan is over.

options.text: It has a very long half-life so it lasts in storage.
options.rationale: Students pick the property that suits a supplier rather than a patient, assuming a long half-life is always the useful one.

options.text: It stays at the same activity for the whole of a scan.
options.rationale: A steady signal sounds ideal for imaging, and students do not connect constant activity with radiation that never dies away in the patient.

mcqs.stem: During radiotherapy, gamma radiation is aimed at a tumour from several different directions. Which statement best explains why?

options.text: Healthy tissue is not affected by gamma radiation at all.
options.rationale: Students believe the beam only acts on the tumour, so they see no problem for the technique to solve.

options.text: Gamma radiation only damages cells where beams overlap.
options.rationale: Students over-read the aiming and invent a threshold rule, assuming a single beam does nothing on its own.

options.text: The tumour gets a high dose while healthy tissue gets less.
options.rationale: Every beam passes through the tumour but each takes a different path through healthy tissue, so the dose concentrates on the tumour.

options.text: It makes the treatment completely free of any risk.
options.rationale: Students think a precaution either removes a risk entirely or is pointless, rather than reducing it.

mcqs.stem: A doctor must decide whether to use a radioactive tracer scan on a patient. Which approach is the best way to evaluate this use of nuclear radiation?

options.text: Refuse it, because every use of radiation carries a risk.
options.rationale: Students treat any radiation risk as absolute and stop the evaluation before the benefits are considered at all.

options.text: Accept it, because medical scans are always safe for patients.
options.rationale: Students who trust that anything a hospital does must be safe skip the evaluation from the other direction.

options.text: Compare the activity in becquerels with the legal limit.
options.rationale: Students who confuse activity with dose look up the wrong quantity, which says nothing about the harm to this patient.

options.text: Weigh the dose received against the benefit of a diagnosis.
options.rationale: Evaluating means setting the measured drawback, the dose and its risk, against the benefit, the information the scan gives about the patient's illness.

mcqs.stem: A hospital leaflet states that a chest scan gives a dose of about 0.1 mSv, and that the average dose from background radiation in the UK is about 2.7 mSv per year. Which conclusion do these data best support?

options.text: The scan adds much less than a year of background dose.
options.rationale: 0.1 mSv is about one twenty-seventh of 2.7 mSv, so the extra dose is a small fraction of what the patient receives from background radiation anyway.

options.text: The scan should be refused because any dose is harmful.
options.rationale: Students judge on the presence of a risk rather than its size, so the numbers in the stem play no part in their answer.

options.text: Background dose is the same for everyone, so this is exact.
options.rationale: Students read a quoted average as a fixed value and forget that occupation and location change it.

options.text: The scan gives about 27 times the yearly background dose.
options.rationale: The student divides the two figures the wrong way round and reports the ratio inverted.

mcqs.stem: Radiotherapy to destroy a tumour also carries a risk of damaging healthy cells. Which statement is the best evaluation of that risk?

options.text: Radiotherapy should never be offered to any patient.
options.rationale: Students who treat radiation risk as absolute reject the treatment without considering what happens if the tumour is left.

options.text: The risk is smaller than that of leaving the cancer.
options.rationale: Evaluating a perceived risk means comparing consequences: damage to some healthy cells is set against the consequences of an untreated tumour.

options.text: There is no risk, since beams reach only the tumour.
options.rationale: Students believe an aimed beam affects nothing on the way in, so they deny that there is any risk to evaluate.

options.text: The risk cannot be judged unless the dose is zero.
options.rationale: Students think an evaluation requires certainty of safety, rather than a comparison of the sizes of two risks.
